ap_calculus_ab-m01.stem: The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, of a liquid is modeled for $0\le t\le 8$ minutes. The graph of $T$ is shown and consists of line segments. Which of the following is a correct interpretation of $T'(7)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of T(t), consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.text: At $t=7$ minutes the temperature is increasing at a rate of $1$ degrees Celsius per minute.
options.why: Reverses the sign: the slope is negative, so the temperature is decreasing.

options.text: At $t=7$ minutes the temperature is decreasing at a rate of $6$ degrees Celsius per minute.
options.why: Uses the height of the graph, T(7) = 6, as the rate of change instead of the slope.

options.text: Between $t=0$ and $t=8$ minutes the temperature changes at an average rate of $\frac{3}{8}$ degrees Celsius per minute.
options.why: Reports the average rate of change over the whole interval, not the instantaneous rate at the given time.

options.text: At $t=7$ minutes the temperature is decreasing at a rate of $1$ degrees Celsius per minute.
options.why: T'(7) is the slope of the graph at t = 7, which is -1, so the temperature is decreasing by 1 degrees Celsius per minute.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Interpret the derivative at a time as an instantaneous rate with units using the slope of a graph
student_thinking: Read the slope of the graph at the given time
Recognize the slope as the instantaneous rate of change of temperature
Match the sign to increasing or decreasing and include the units

key_conditions.condition: T'(a) is the slope of the segment containing t = a, because a lies inside a segment
key_conditions.evidence: t is an odd integer, never a vertex

misconceptions.description: uses the average rate over the whole interval

verification.independent_path: difference quotient of the interpolated graph at t = a +/- 1e-6 (independent of the vertex list)

ap_calculus_ab-m02.stem: Let $f(x)=3\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$. The graph of the function $g$, which consists of line segments, is shown for $0\le x\le 6$. If $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)$, what is the absolute maximum value of $h$ on the interval $[0,6]$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Reports the x-coordinate where the maximum occurs instead of the maximum value.
Candidates: endpoints, the corners of g (where h' does not exist) and solutions of f'(x) = g'(x) on each segment; h is evaluated at each with a calculator and the largest value is chosen.
Reports h(6), the right endpoint value.
Maximizes f alone and subtracts g only at the endpoints.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find an absolute maximum of f - g where g is a graph with corners, using the candidates test
student_thinking: Recognize that h' does not exist at the corners of g and that h' = f' - g' on each segment
Solve f'(x) = slope of g on each segment and list the corners and endpoints as candidates
Evaluate h at each candidate with a calculator and compare

key_conditions.condition: h is continuous on a closed interval so the absolute maximum occurs at an endpoint, a corner or a critical point

verification.independent_path: maximum of h over a 6001-point grid on [0, 6] (independent of the candidate list)

ap_calculus_ab-m03.stem: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x/4}$. The graph of the function $g$, which consists of line segments, is shown. If $q(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, what is the value of $q'(1)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Reverses the numerator: f g' - f' g.
q'(a) = (f'(a) g(a) - f(a) g'(a)) / g(a)^2; g(a) and g'(a) come from the graph and f(a), f'(a) from the formula (calculator).
Divides the numerator by g(a) instead of g(a) squared.
Divides the derivatives, f'(a)/g'(a), instead of using the quotient rule.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Apply the quotient rule at a point when the numerator is a formula and the denominator is a graph
student_thinking: Differentiate the formula and evaluate f(a), f'(a) with a calculator
Read g(a) and the slope g'(a) from the graph
Apply the quotient rule with the numerator in the right order

key_conditions.condition: g(a) is not zero and g is differentiable at a because a is interior to a segment
key_conditions.evidence: g(a) is a positive integer read from the graph

misconceptions.description: divides by g instead of g squared

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of the lambdified formula divided by the interpolated graph (independent of the quotient rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m04.stem: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x/4}$. The graph of the function $g$, which consists of line segments, is shown. If $h(x)=f(x)\,g(x)$, what is the value of $h''(1)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Puts the derivative factors in the wrong places: f''(a) g'(a) + 2 f'(a) g(a).
h'' = f'' g + 2 f' g' + f g''; on a line segment g'' = 0, so h''(a) = f''(a) g(a) + 2 f'(a) g'(a), with g(a) and g'(a) read from the graph.
Returns the first derivative h'(a) = f'(a) g(a) + f(a) g'(a).
Leaves out the middle term 2 f'(a) g'(a) because g'' = 0 on a segment, but the product rule for second derivatives still has it.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Compute a second derivative of a product where one factor is a graph made of line segments
student_thinking: Apply the product rule twice to get h'' = f'' g + 2 f' g' + f g''
Use g'' = 0 on a line segment and read g(a), g'(a) from the graph
Evaluate f' and f'' at a with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: g is linear near x = a so g''(a) = 0
key_conditions.evidence: a is interior to a segment of the graph

misconceptions.description: puts the derivatives in the wrong places

verification.independent_path: second central difference (step 1e-4) of the product of the lambdified formula and the interpolated graph (independent of the product rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m05.stem: The function $y=f(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=g(x)\,y$ with $f(0)=2$, where the graph of $g$, consisting of line segments, is shown. What is the value of $f(8)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Adds the area instead of exponentiating: y(0) + integral of g.
Uses g(8) in the exponent instead of the integral of g from 0 to 8.
Separating variables gives ln|y| = integral of g, so f(8) = f(0) e^{integral of g from 0 to 8}; the integral is the signed area under the graph and e to that power needs a calculator.
Multiplies y(0) by the integral of g instead of by e to that power.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Solve dy/dx = g(x) y by separation of variables when g is given as a graph
student_thinking: Separate variables to get ln|y| equal to the integral of g
Evaluate the integral as signed area read from the graph
Use the initial condition and evaluate the exponential with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: y stays positive because f(0) > 0 and the solution is y(0) exp(integral of g)

verification.independent_path: Runge-Kutta numerical integration of the differential equation with the interpolated g (independent of separation of variables)

ap_calculus_ab-m06.stem: The graph of the function $f$, consisting of line segments, is shown. The trapezoidal sum with the three subintervals determined by the points $x=0,2,4,8$ is used to approximate $\int_0^8 f(x)\,dx$. What is the value of this approximation?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses the exact area under the graph of f instead of the trapezoidal sum for the given subintervals.
Treats the three subintervals as if they had equal width 8/3.
Trapezoidal sum = sum of (f(left) + f(right))/2 times the width of each subinterval, using the values read from the graph.
Uses left endpoints with the given subinterval widths instead of trapezoids.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Compute a trapezoidal sum with unequal subinterval widths using values read from a graph
student_thinking: Read f at each of the four given points from the graph
Find the width of each subinterval
Apply (left + right)/2 times width on each subinterval and add

key_conditions.condition: the trapezoidal rule applies on each subinterval separately, so unequal widths are allowed

verification.independent_path: direct sum of the numerically interpolated heights times widths (independent of exact rationals)
